title: Rate Limiter: Complete Architecture
description: Design a high-performance rate limiter with monolith and microservice architectures using React, ASP.NET Core, Azure, and AWS.

data.text: Design a distributed rate limiter that protects APIs and microservices from abuse. It must support multiple rate-limiting algorithms (token bucket, sliding window, fixed window), enforce limits by user ID, IP address, or API endpoint, allow hot-reloading of rules without restart, and serve rate-limit decisions in under 1 millisecond — all while scaling horizontally to handle 1 million requests per second at the data plane.

data.title: Functional Requirements
items: Support token bucket algorithm: allows burst up to bucket capacity, refills at a steady rate per second
Support sliding window log: track precise request timestamps within the window duration
Support sliding window counter: approximate O(1) counter-based sliding window with weighted average
Support fixed window counter: simplest algorithm with hard reset at window boundaries
Rate-limit key strategies: by authenticated user ID, by client IP address, by API endpoint + method, or composite keys (user + endpoint)
Tiered rate plans: Free tier (100 req/min), Pro tier (1000 req/min), Enterprise (custom), each applied per key
Hot-reload rate limit rules: API Gateway picks up rule changes within 5 seconds without restart
Return standard rate-limit headers: X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset, Retry-After
Bypass list: allowlisted API keys, internal service mesh traffic, and health-check endpoints are exempt
Per-rule configuration: burst allowance, window duration, and penalty duration for repeated violators

data.title: Non-Functional Requirements
items: Sub-1ms latency for the rate-limit decision at P99 — the data plane must not add measurable API latency
99.99% availability: rate-limit checks must never block or crash the protected API path
Horizontal scalability to 1M+ rate-limit decisions per second per data-plane instance
Rule propagation latency under 5 seconds from config store to all gateway instances
Distributed consistency: counters sharded by key must not over-count across multiple gateway nodes
Graceful degradation: if Redis is unreachable, default to allow (fail-open) or deny (fail-closed) based on configured policy
Observability: per-rule violation metrics, per-client usage percentiles, and rule hit-rate dashboards

data.text: Start with an ASP.NET Core middleware that intercepts every HTTP request before it reaches the controller. Rate-limit state is stored in a local in-memory ConcurrentDictionary keyed by rate-limit key. Rules are loaded once at startup from a JSON config file. This validates algorithm correctness and middleware pipeline integration before introducing distributed state.

data.title: Monolith Tech Stack
data.code:
Frontend:
  - React 18 with TypeScript
  - Vite for build tooling
  - Tailwind CSS for styling
  - React Query for server state

Backend (ASP.NET Core Monolith):
  - Custom RateLimitMiddleware registered first in the pipeline
  - In-memory ConcurrentDictionary<string, TokenBucket> for per-key counters
  - IOptionsMonitor<RateLimitRules> for hot-reload of JSON config file
  - System.Threading.SemaphoreSlim to serialize Redis writes in the distributed path
  - Serilog with rate-limit event enrichment for violation logging
  - Rules: List<RateLimitRule> loaded from appsettings.ratelimit.json at startup

Infrastructure:
  - Azure App Service or AWS ECS single-service deployment
  - Redis (Azure Cache / ElastiCache) for shared state in the distributed path
  - Single in-memory state — not suitable for multi-instance deployments

data.text: The rate limiter data plane is best deployed as an API Gateway plugin or sidecar — it must be on the hot path. Split the supporting control plane into three microservices: RuleService manages rules, ConfigService distributes rules to gateways via Redis Pub/Sub, and AnalyticsService aggregates violation metrics. The decision logic itself is a Lua script executed atomically on Redis, giving sub-millisecond P99 latency.

items: RateCheckService (Data Plane): The actual rate-limit evaluation engine. In production, this is not a remote service call — it is a Lua script running on Redis invoked by the API Gateway or Envoy sidecar. The script receives the rate-limit key and rule ID, performs the algorithm atomically, and returns { allowed, remaining, resetAt }. For the monolith demo, this is the ASP.NET Core middleware calling Redis directly.

RuleService (Control Plane): CRUD API for rate limit rules. Each rule has: id, keyStrategy (userId, ip, endpoint, composite), algorithm (tokenBucket, slidingWindowLog, slidingWindowCounter, fixedWindow), limit, windowSeconds, burstCapacity, planTier. Rules are versioned; publishing a new version does not affect active rules until explicitly promoted. Exposes a REST API consumed by the admin dashboard.

ConfigService (Control Plane): Distributes the active rule snapshot to all gateway instances. Uses Redis Pub/Sub to push rule-update events. Each gateway subscribes and atomically swaps the in-memory rule dictionary. Falls back to polling Redis every 30 seconds if the Pub/Sub connection drops. Manages the rule promotion lifecycle (draft → active → deprecated).

AnalyticsService (Control Plane): Aggregates violation events streamed from all gateways via Kafka. Computes per-client, per-endpoint, and per-rule metrics: total requests, blocked count, block rate %, P99 latency of the rate-limit check itself. Powers the admin dashboard with Prometheus + Grafana or Azure Monitor Workbooks. Detects rule misconfigurations (e.g., a rule blocking 100% of traffic).

KeyResolverService (Control Plane): Resolves the composite rate-limit key from the incoming request context. A single request may produce multiple keys (e.g., key for user tier + key for endpoint + key for IP). The KeyResolver inspects the authenticated user JWT, the X-Forwarded-For header, and the request path/method, then returns an ordered list of keys and their matching rule IDs.

data.title: React App Structure
data.code:
src/
  features/
    RateLimiter/
      components/
        RuleEditor/        # Create/edit rules: algorithm picker, tier selector
        RuleTable/         # List rules with status (draft/active/deprecated), version
        ViolationChart/    # Time-series chart of blocked requests per rule
        ClientUsageTable/  # Per-client usage heatmap showing limit vs remaining
        HotReloadIndicator/# Live dot showing last config-push timestamp per gateway
      hooks/
        useRateLimitRules.ts    # React Query infinite list with real-time WebSocket updates
        useViolationMetrics.ts  # Polls analytics endpoint, feeds Recharts
        useRulePromotion.ts     # Mutation + optimistic rule promotion with rollback
      pages/
        RulesPage.tsx           # Rule CRUD, promote/demote workflow
        AnalyticsPage.tsx        # Dashboard: violations, top blocked clients, rule efficiency
        GatewaysPage.tsx         # Gateway instance health, rule version per instance
      store/
        rule-store.ts           # Zustand: draft rules, active rule snapshot, promotion queue
      types/
        rule.ts                 # RateLimitRule, Algorithm, KeyStrategy, PlanTier
  shared/
    ui/
    lib/
    hooks/

Key Patterns:
  - useRateLimitRules subscribes to WebSocket for live rule push events
  - RuleEditor validates algorithm-specific constraints before saving (e.g. burst <= limit for token bucket)
  - ViolationChart uses Recharts with 1-second refresh for ops dashboards
  - HotReloadIndicator turns red if any gateway has not acknowledged the latest rule version in >10s

data.title: Token Bucket Lua Script for Redis (Sub-1ms Data Plane)

cards.title: Rate Limit (Data Plane)
cards.description: Enforce rate limits at the edge or API gateway layer with minimal added latency
pros: Azure APIM supports quota-by-key and rate-limit-by-key policies declaratively
AWS API Gateway usage plans + throttles are natively IAM-integrated
cons: APIM standard tier has a 4ms baseline overhead per call
API Gateway per-region account limits require support ticket to raise

cards.title: Distributed Config
cards.description: Distribute active rate-limit rules to all gateway nodes within 5 seconds
pros: App Configuration push via Event Grid triggers rule reload in <5s
AppConfig validates JSON schemas before deploying a configuration
cons: Polling fallback required if push delivery is interrupted

cards.title: Cache
cards.description: Token bucket and sliding window counters stored as Redis data structures with Lua CAS
pros: Lua script execution is single-threaded and atomic — perfect for CAS counters
Redis Cluster mode shards keys across nodes for 1M+ ops/sec
cons: Keyspace eviction (maxmemory-policy) can lose rate-limit state during memory pressure

cards.title: Event Streaming
cards.description: Stream violation and usage events from gateways to AnalyticsService
pros: Event Hubs Capture auto-writes to ADLS for long-term violation audit
Kinesis Data Firehose delivers metrics directly to CloudWatch
cons: Throughput provisioning must be sized for peak request volume

cards.title: Dashboard / Observability
cards.description: Real-time violation rate dashboards and per-rule efficiency metrics
pros: Application Insights automatically correlates rate-limit 429s with downstream service health
Managed Grafana pre-built dashboards for API Gateway throttles
cons: Grafana alert rules need separate maintenance from infrastructure IaC

data.title: When to Choose Microservices?
data.text: Start with a monolith. Split into microservices only when you have clear scaling bottlenecks, independent deployment needs, or team boundaries that justify the operational overhead.

data.title: Summary
points: The rate-limit data plane must be sub-1ms — use a Redis Lua script, not a remote service call
Token bucket is the best general-purpose algorithm: it allows controlled bursts while maintaining a steady rate
Shard rate-limit keys across Redis cluster nodes to horizontally scale past a single Redis instance
Distribute rules via Redis Pub/Sub with a polling fallback — 5-second propagation is achievable
The control plane (RuleService, ConfigService, AnalyticsService) is separated from the data plane to keep the hot path lean
Graceful degradation (fail-open vs fail-closed) must be a configurable policy, not an accidental behavior
data.takeaway: Rate limiter design is a study in separating the ultra-fast data plane (Redis Lua, sub-1ms) from the management control plane (rules CRUD, analytics). Token bucket with Redis CAS counters, hot-pushed rule configuration, and multi-key sharding are the three decisions that determine whether your rate limiter adds measurable latency or disappears into the network.
